title: Sardis (Revelation 3:1–6)
hook: you have a name for being alive, but wake up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thyatira: a church whose latest works were more than its first. Your line was more than at first.

A cliff so steep the guards didn't bother watching it. That's the story the old Greek historian Herodotus tells about the citadel of Sardis: an enemy soldier saw a defender climb down the rock to fetch a fallen helmet, noticed the way up nobody was guarding, and the city fell. Some readers hear that story behind today's letter; others say it needs no backstory. Either way, its opening lands like an alarm. The risen Christ tells the church in Sardis: everyone thinks you're alive. You aren't. Wake up.

First, the verdict, in the King James words: "I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead." A name for being alive: a good reputation, a full calendar, people who'd say this church is thriving. Notice what's missing. No persecution named, no false teacher. Just a church asleep inside its own good name. Second, what to do: "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die." Not start over. Like a fire nearly out: you don't build a new one, you blow on the embers still red. Then: "Remember therefore how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent." Go back to how it began. Third, the warning: "If therefore thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know what hour I will come upon thee." It echoes Jesus in the Gospels: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come." A thief doesn't send a calendar invite. Fourth, the tender part: "Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white." Even in a sleeping church, some are awake, and the letter counts them. And whoever overcomes, their name will not be blotted out of the book of life. So Sardis sets two names side by side: the name a church has with everyone else, and the name kept in the book of life. The letter cares about the second.

Choose something right around you that you've stopped noticing, the sound of the room, the weight of your hands, the light on a wall, and meet it as if for the first time. When your mind drifts back to sleep, and it will, wake up to it again; that's all watchfulness is, one return at a time. If you pray, ask to be kept awake; if not, just keep returning.
Sardis. The church with a name for being alive, told to wake up and strengthen what remains, with a few in white who never fell asleep.
Your line: wake up. The embers are still red, and there's something left to blow on. That's today.

howItsDone: Christians use the language of watchfulness and waking up in sermons and prayers, and some churches read the Gospel warnings to keep watch in Advent.

chat.says: Our church looks great from outside. Packed calendar. What could Sardis's letter possibly say to us?
options: Sardis had a name for being alive but was asleep; the letter says wake up, strengthen what remains.
Sardis was praised for its busy calendar, since a good name proves a church is alive.
Sardis was told to tear everything down and start over with brand-new people.
chat.meaning: Sardis had "a name that thou livest, and art dead." The letter says wake up and strengthen what remains, and counts a few still awake.

Sardis.meaning: the city whose church got Revelation's fifth letter

book of life.meaning: the book where the overcomers' names are kept
